title: Nettle and the Quiet Nudge
markdown:
High Perch clung to cliff sides like colourful mushrooms: ochre, crimson, sky-blue roofs, spiderweb bridges over green gorges, a market on sunny ledges selling silks, polished stones, and jars of fungi that glowed even by day. Mountains ticked the clouds. The air smelled of stone-warmth and spiced honey cake. Merchants called without quite shouting. Children practised pebble-throws into buckets, not gorges.

In a cottage built into the softest hillside lived Nettle, an ogre the colour of moss after rain, eyes like warm pebbles. He was not fond of stomping. He moved as if the world had asked him not to hurry. His kettle knew him. His garden knew him. On his shoulder, or in a wool-lined basket, rode Pudding: a snowy puff of kitten with cornflower eyes, a purr like a tiny motor, a tail that twitched at secrets. She patrolled windowsills the way some cats patrol kingdoms.

“Pudding is quite the treasure,” Nettle would rumble, soft as a meadow breeze rustling a hillside. Pudding mewed and rubbed his green thumb, white tail ticking like a small delighted clock. Neighbours who hurried past still found themselves slowing, which Nettle never mentioned.

Every year came the Gorge Games: rope-dancers, pebble-throwers, friendly show-off. This year a golden-willow whistle promised good weather. Nettle felt a peculiar gentle nudge to try—not for the whistle, for a quiet test of his own cleverness. He did not want to try too hard. That was not his way.

The day dawned without a cloud. He ambled to the square, Pudding in the basket, tummy rumbling at honey cakes. Bunting had been strung from ledge to ledge as if the gorge itself were invited. Two spellcasters had been invited to judge. Professor Puff, tall and thin, nose like a pointed hat, booming voice, believed in smoke and glitter. Madame Twinkle, shorter, rounder, spectacles like dewdrops, favoured moonlight patterns and pizzazz. Between them they could fill a valley with compliments that were also arguments.

“A Spectacle of Skill!” Puff’s voice shook peaks and scattered birds. “Judged on Style Points!”

Twinkle clapped; pink and silver sparks. “Precision, panache, pizzazz! Gasps, not polite nods!”

Nettle blinked. He had thought of baking a loaf that rose properly, or mending a frayed bridge with a sturdy knot. These people were loud. The air crackled in a way the gorge did not usually ask for. Pudding’s ears flattened a fraction, then rose again, working.

Fidget the goblin darted through, pointy ears twitching. “I am not lost,” he told a shopper with apples. “I am taking the scenic route with conviction. Though this route has a great deal of sparkly noise and not enough sensible mushrooms.” He paused, darting-eyed, then scurried toward a burst of magic, weaving near the viewing-ledge edges as if the drop were a rumour he had not yet believed.

Puff conjured rainbow water that ran uphill and became a dancing dragon breathing lavender smoke. “Eight-point-five for fluidity. Nine for audaciousness.”

Twinkle wove moonlight into a tapestry of High Perch’s history. “Quite pretty, dear Professor. Lacking celestial grace. That dragon looked wobbly. Too much fizzy berry juice. Seven-point-two, and that’s generous.”

They glared. Tinder, wind. Nettle’s brow creased. Pudding was not watching dragons. She watched the gorge-edge, where children and Fidget leaned on a rail. Cliff-side flowers drooped. The air trembled. A loose stone at the main ledge wobbled with every boom and every goblin skitter.

Nettle could have spelled the stone still. He could have shouted. He would have become the event, and events, in High Perch, tended to grow extra verses. That wasn’t his way. Quiet was his way. He leaned to the basket.

“You see something, don’t you, my little Pudding?”

A confident chirp. He took out a perfectly round mountain apple that tasted of sunshine and tossed it, underhand, onto soft moss away from the children, away from the stone. Not a flourish. A roll. The sort of throw you use when you do not wish the mountain to notice.

Thump. Pudding became a white blur, hunter’s instinct, dancer’s feet. She pounced with such quiet focus that her paws, landing, gave the loose stone a tiny controlled shift. It wobbled—then settled with a soft, reassuring thud instead of a crash into green air.

Children looked. Fidget’s eyes went wide. They saw the drop. They scrambled back. Fidget hid behind a rock, alarm and new caution sharing his face.

Pudding trotted back, tail a banner, and nibbled the apple with delicate precision. Puff grumbled, “Minor disruption. Poor audience control.”

Twinkle watched the kitten crunch. “Observe the feline’s poise. Focus. Quiet competence.” Her gaze found Nettle.

He stepped forward without a flourish. He picked up a fallen bloom, straightened its stem, and set it where it could catch sun, the same care he used on Pudding’s fur. No one asked him for a score. He would not have known where to write it.

Villagers saw a large ogre do a small repair. They saw a small kitten prevent a large fall. A rope-dancer, mid-stretch, forgot to show off. A pebble-thrower put his pebble back in his pocket. The spellcasters’ competitive glint thinned, as if someone had opened a window in a room full of smoke.

“Remarkably simple,” Puff muttered, quill hovering. “No grand illusions. Just fixing.”

“A quiet mastery of the fundamental,” Twinkle said, and the smile reached her spectacles. Their pads began to collect words like practicality and gentle precision.

Judging shifted—kindness, sensible knots, heartfelt skill. A girl showed a loaf that had risen without fireworks. A boy demonstrated a bridge-knot you could trust in wind. Nettle did not win the whistle. He did not get the score they had invented that morning. The cheer that came was warmer than any gasp, and Fidget, from behind his rock, joined it a beat late, which was still a kind of conviction.

Sunset painted peaks orange and lavender. Honey cakes passed from hand to hand. Cider steamed. The spellcasters, no longer a duel, conjured lights that twinkled without bullying the dusk, small as fireflies and twice as polite. Nettle sat on moss-rock, Pudding a motor in his lap, tail thumping now and then. He scratched the spot behind her ear that always worked. The gorge went quiet, as gorges prefer. Someone offered him the whistle anyway, as a joke or a gift. He shook his head. Weather, in High Perch, could look after itself for one night.

Later, rain tapped his cottage window. Steam rose from evening tea. Pudding’s paws, still a little mossy, tucked in. Nettle thought of her quiet bravery the way he thought of bread: without announcing it. He did not make a speech to the mug. He watched the first bead of rain travel down the glass, slow as an ogre, sure as a kitten’s nudge, and let the day settle without a score. Outside, High Perch’s bridges held. The loose stone held. That was enough pizzazz for one gorge.
characters: Nettle (gentle hillside ogre), Pudding (fluffy white kitten), Fidget (scenic-route goblin)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
